intro:
Use it to show how a value moved over time: visits per week, response time per hour. Each row of `data` is a point, and each `LineChart.Line` is a series drawn from one of its keys.

The grid, the fill, the axes, the legend and the readout are separate parts, so a chart has only the ones you write.

The value axis fits the data and does not have to reach zero, so a small change stays visible. To compare sizes, use a [bar chart](/docs/web/charts/bar-chart).

parts.Header: The strip above the plot: `title`, `value` and `caption`, with the series key or your own control on the trailing side.
parts.Grid: Lines across the value axis, in the theme's border colour. `rows` is roughly how many: the axis picks round numbers near it.
parts.Area: The fill under a series, fading to nothing at the bottom of the plot. It always draws under the lines.
parts.Line: One series. Declare one per key. A later `Line` draws over an earlier one.
parts.ReferenceLine: A rule across the plot at the value `y`: a budget, an average, a target. It counts toward the value axis, and `label` writes text above its left end.
parts.Marker: A rule down the plot at the row `index`: a release, the day something ran out. `label` writes text beside its top.
parts.Skeleton: A flat rule where the series will be, with a highlight moving along it, drawn only while `status` is `loading`.
parts.XAxis: The x labels, each on its own point. `ticks` is how many, evenly spaced with both ends kept.
parts.YAxis: Value labels on the grid lines, in round numbers, with room made for them.
parts.Legend: A swatch and a name per line, over the top corner of the plot. On a chart with a header, use the header's `legend` prop instead.
parts.Tooltip: The readout, and what drives it. It adds the crosshair and a dot on every line, and it covers the plot, so the pointer can be anywhere. `showLabel={false}` drops the popover.

examples.title: Two series
examples.description: Declare a `Line` per series. They share one value axis, so they stay comparable. The header's `legend` prop names them.

examples.title: Actual and forecast
examples.description: `dashArray` draws a projection, and `showMarkers` puts a dot on every point of a short series. Repeat the last actual value in the forecast's column so the two lines meet. `curve="linear"` joins the points straight.

examples.title: Steps against a plan
examples.description: `curve="step"` on one `Line` holds each value until the next, for a balance that moves on the day money does. The other line keeps the chart's curve, so a smooth plan can sit beside it.

examples.title: Marking a value and a row
examples.description: `ReferenceLine` marks a value, such as an average, and `Marker` marks a row. The axis grows to include a reference line above or below the data.

examples.title: Any colour
examples.description: `color` takes a theme role or any CSS colour, for a chart whose colour comes from elsewhere in your app. A row can carry extra fields, and `XAxis.format` and `Tooltip.formatX` get the whole row, so here an estimated value says so.

examples.title: Missing values
examples.description: A row with no number for a series leaves a gap in that line. Over a gap, the readout moves to the nearest point with a value.

examples.title: Sparkline
examples.description: `compact` drops the axis padding so the line reaches the edges. With no `Tooltip` it does not take focus, so give it a `label` that says what the shape shows.

examples.title: Loading, then data
examples.description: Add `LineChart.Skeleton` and drive `status`. The series draws in from the left when it turns `ready`, and again each time it goes back to `loading` and returns.

examples.title: Changing data
examples.description: When `data` changes, the points and the axis move to their new values over `domainDuration`, and the reveal does not play again. A `ref` on the chart has `replay()`, which runs it on demand.

notes:
### Sizing

The chart fills its container's width and takes its height from `aspectRatio`, which applies to the plot alone, so a header does not shrink it. The plot draws in the browser after it has been measured, and the space is reserved until then, so it is not in server-rendered HTML.

### The value axis

The derived axis spans every `Line` and `Area`, with some headroom, rounded to numbers worth labelling. `yDomain` fixes it, which is the way to hold it steady across charts or to bring zero in.

### Bundle size

The chart adds about 65 KB of gzipped JavaScript to a page that uses it. A page that does not import it pays nothing, including one that imports other components from the package root.

### Colour

`color` on any part takes a role in the theme or any CSS colour. A role follows light and dark on its own, and a CSS colour stays as you give it. Every series defaults to `chart-1`, so give the others their own.

### Reading a point

With a `Tooltip`, hovering the plot reads the nearest point. A click or a tap pins the reading until the next press elsewhere, or Escape. On a touch screen a sideways drag reads the points it crosses, and a vertical drag scrolls the page.

`onActiveIndexChange` fires when the point changes, not on every frame, so it can drive a readout outside the chart, as the first example does. Inside the chart, `useLineChart` gives the same point.

### Keyboard

With a `Tooltip`, the plot takes focus. The arrow keys move between points, Home and End go to the first and last, Enter or Space pins the reading, and Escape clears it.

### Screen readers

Each row is given as text beside the drawing. `label` names the chart and `labelForDatum` writes a row, for values with a unit. Without them a row is read as its keys and values.

### Reduced motion

With reduced motion set, the series and the axis appear at their final values, and the skeleton's highlight is not drawn.
propsNote: `LineChart`, `LineChart.Header` and `LineChart.Legend` also take the props of the element they render, and a `className`. `LineChart.Tooltip` puts its `className` on the readout. The other parts draw nothing themselves and take only the props listed.
